price.note: Voting share. The non-voting share (TKYO.X0000) closed at Rs 67.40 the same day; both classes have the same rights to profit and dividends, so the same fair value applies to each.

summary.headline: Sri Lanka's biggest cement maker, selling more than ever, but profit is falling, debt is high and at Rs 81.70 (Rs 67.40 non-voting) the share is about four times fair value
summary.text:
Tokyo Cement makes cement in Trincomalee (4 Mn MT a year of capacity) and ready-mix concrete, aggregates and dry mortar, with its own biomass and solar power. Sales are booming: cement volume rose 28% in 2025/26 and revenue rose 27% in April–September 2026. But the industry has not raised prices while costs, freight and the rupee moved against it, so profit fell: Rs 1.50bn in the half against Rs 1.67bn, and twelve-month return on equity is only 7.7%.

Fair value is about **Rs 19.35** (buy below **Rs 16.45**, strong buy below **Rs 14.51**), down from Rs 45.00 in the first analysis. The main reason is the house required return: with a beta of 1.19 (cement relevered for Rs 15.6bn of net debt) the cost of equity is 20.5%, against 15.5% assumed before. A business earning 8–11% on its equity is worth well below its Rs 72.51 book value at that rate; today's price needs a long-run ROE of about 22% (19% for the non-voting share).

Only 1 of the 4 business tests passes (debt). Category 3, avoid for now: unchanged. The non-voting share is the cheaper class if the view changes.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages (Rs 10.78 / 18.33 / 34.74) of five methods: whole-company DCF, P/E, justified P/B, residual income and the dividend model. NAV Rs 72.51 is shown for reference, not averaged. Same value for both share classes.

methodReadings.reading: Price is 1.13× NAV (non-voting 0.93×). Most assets are the Trincomalee plant, the vessel and stock; land is at cost.
Well below the 20.5% cost of equity. Justified P/B at an 11% long-run ROE is 0.39×; today's price needs about 22%.
On twelve-month EPS Rs 5.45. Justified forward P/E is about 3.5× at the base case (payout 55%, cost of equity 20.5%, growth 5%).
Rs 2.50 is 43% of 2025/26 profit, but free cash flow was negative in 2025/26 and the twelve months to Sep 2026; the dividend has been paid partly with borrowed money.
At a 16% WACC the operating business is worth about Rs 16bn, barely more than the Rs 15.6bn of net debt. The return on capital (8–10%) is below WACC, so growth adds little value.

models.name: Whole-company DCF
models.comment: Whole-company DCF at WACC 17.1% / 16.0% / 15.0%: after-tax operating profit Rs 2.94 / 3.27 / 3.27bn (twelve months to Sep 2026, Rs 4.68bn taxed at 30.1%; bear 10% lower), start cash after maintenance capex Rs 3.08 / 3.40 / 4.25bn, growth 2% / 6% / 9% for five years then 4% / 5% / 6%, return on new capital 8% / 10% / 13%; less net debt Rs 15.57bn (30 Sep 2026). Debt is 31% of the company's value and almost equals the firm value in the bear case, so the equity swings from below zero (bear Rs −2.94: a share can't be worth less than nothing, but the figure is kept as calculated) to Rs 39.88 (bull). About 65% and 74% of the base and bull values come after year 5.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: EPS to March 2027 Rs 5.20 / 6.20 / 6.80 (six months Rs 3.41; last year's second half Rs 2.04, hit by Cyclone Ditwah) × justified P/E 2.8 / 3.5 / 4.4 (payout 1 − growth ÷ ROE at long-run ROE 8% / 11% / 14%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%, cost of equity 22.0% / 20.5% / 19.0%). The base is 21% below the Rs 7.84 run-rate (September quarter × 4) because July–September is the seasonal peak: it gave 39% of 2025/26's EPS.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: NAV Rs 72.51 (30 Sep 2026) × (long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth): ROE 8% / 11% / 14%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%. Justified P/B 0.22 / 0.39 / 0.62 against 1.13 today.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book Rs 72.51; ROE moving from 7.7% (twelve months to Sep 2026) to 8% / 11% / 14% over ten years; 43% payout; then excess returns grow at 4% / 5% / 6%.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Next dividend Rs 2.00 / 2.50 / 2.75 (Rs 2.50 paid for 2025/26; bear cut because cash after capex hasn't covered it), growing 2% / 5% / 8% for five years, then the stable payout 1 − growth ÷ ROE at long-run ROE 8% / 11% / 14% and growth 4% / 5% / 6%, at the cost of equity.

modelsNote: Five methods are averaged in each scenario: whole-company DCF, P/E, justified price to book, residual income and the dividend model. Growth check: 2% / 6% / 9% against 15.1% supported by 2025/26 reinvestment (186% of after-tax operating profit, swollen by Rs 3.66bn of stock and receivables and the vessel) at an 8.1% return on capital; all within. Maintenance capex: the company gives no split. 2025/26 capex booked of Rs 4.81bn was mostly growth (Rs 3.37bn for the Trinco Express vessel and dry docking), so bear and base use depreciation as reported (Rs 2.29bn) rather than the one-year capex the calculator offers as its bear; bull uses capex less the vessel (Rs 1.44bn). Ratio notes: the beta of 1.19 is high for a cement maker because net debt is 46% of market value; the 15.0× trailing P/E is above the 8–12× range for a mature business because the market expects margins to recover. Warnings: dividends are more than cash after maintenance capex (dividend at risk), and the expansion was largely borrowed (net debt up Rs 4.4bn in 2025/26).

scenarios.common: Required return from CAPM with a country premium: risk-free 8.24% (12.24% bond less 4.0% default spread), mature premium 4.2% plus country premium 6.08%, beta 1.19. Weights bear 30 / base 50 / bull 20. Net debt Rs 15.57bn and NAV Rs 72.51 at 30 Sep 2026; 441.045mn shares (voting and non-voting together).

sensitivity.title: Residual income, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Starting ROE 7.7%, growth 5%, payout 43%. Rs 81.70 needs a long-run ROE near 22% at the base cost of equity; Rs 67.40 (non-voting) about 19%. The company has reached that in only two of the last six years.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 8,514 in total, against Rs 40,850 for 500 voting shares at Rs 81.70 (Rs 33,700 non-voting at Rs 67.40). Category 3: the tiers show where value is, not a plan to buy now. If buying at all, the non-voting share gives the same profit and dividend for 18% less.
buyPlan.realism: Not realistic. The buy price Rs 16.45 is 80% below the voting price and 76% below the non-voting price. The lowest prices in the last 18 months were Rs 68.00 voting and Rs 58.00 non-voting (2025/26), and Rs 78.50 / 59.60 in April–September 2026.

higher: Cement prices rising enough to lift the gross margin back above 32% and ROE towards 15% or more.
Inventories falling back from Rs 10.9bn, releasing cash to repay the Rs 16.9bn of borrowings and cut interest.
Higher use of the 4 Mn MT plant (about 45% used in 2025/26) as housing and post-cyclone rebuilding pick up.
A lower required return: a falling bond yield or a lower beta as debt falls.
lower: Price competition from importers and the other three local makers in an oversupplied market (10.7 Mn MT of capacity against 5.6 Mn MT of demand).
A weaker rupee or higher freight and fuel costs (imported clinker, Middle East shipping).
Short-term borrowings (Rs 12.6bn current) refinanced at higher rates.
The dividend kept up with borrowed money while cash flow stays weak.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the annual report to March 2026 and the interim reports to June and September 2026. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

quality.reason: Debt is within the limit, but returns are low, there was a loss in 2021/22 and profit is not turning into cash.

management.takeaway: Management chose volume over price: sales grew far faster than the industry, but flat prices, rising costs and the interest on the expansion cut profit, and they expect the new capacity and vessel to pay off only as demand fills the plant.

said.text: Cement volume rose 28% to 1.82 Mn MT against industry growth of 19%, the best year since the 2022 crisis.
The industry kept retail prices unchanged despite higher costs, so profit after tax fell 25% while revenue rose 22%.
Finance costs rose 48% to Rs 1.5bn as the Trincomalee expansion and the vessel came into use.
Local raw materials, 24 MW of own renewable power and coastal shipping softened the rise in fuel, freight and import costs.
The technical partnership with Mitsubishi UBE Cement was renewed for five more years.

Keep investing in people, technology and modern manufacturing.
Ready-mix arm to add plastering, screed mortar and concrete-repair services.
Asks for tax and policy support for first-time home builders to revive housing demand.

Capital spending approved by the directors but not yet provided for.
Turnkey mobile batching plant for the ready-mix business.
Manufactured sand production started at the Mihintale aggregate plant.

fullText:
**Tokyo Cement Company (Lanka) PLC: voting TKYO.N0000 and non-voting TKYO.X0000**
Analysis of 28 November 2026, rebuilt from the 2025/26 annual report and the interim reports to June and September 2026. Prices: Rs 81.70 voting, Rs 67.40 non-voting (CSE closes, 27 November 2026).

**Summary**
Tokyo Cement is Sri Lanka's largest cement maker (4 Mn MT a year at Trincomalee, about a third of the country's 10.7 Mn MT of capacity), with ready-mix concrete, aggregates, dry mortar and its own biomass and solar power. Demand is recovering fast: the company sold 28% more cement in 2025/26 and revenue rose 27% in April–September 2026. Profit has gone the other way. The industry has held prices while clinker, freight, fuel and the rupee moved against it, and the expansion and the new coastal vessel added depreciation and interest. Profit attributable to owners was Rs 2.57bn in 2025/26 (Rs 3.45bn) and Rs 1.50bn in the half (Rs 1.67bn).

Fair value is **Rs 19.35** a share (buy below **Rs 16.45**, strong buy below **Rs 14.51**), the same for both classes. That is far below both prices, and below the first analysis (Rs 45.00), mainly because the house required return is now built from a beta: 1.19 for a cement maker carrying Rs 15.6bn of net debt gives a cost of equity of 20.5% (15.5% was assumed before). At that rate a company earning 8–11% on its equity is worth well under its book value of Rs 72.51. The voting price implies a long-run ROE of about 22%, the non-voting price about 19%; the company reached that in two of the last six years.

Business tests: 1 of 4 (debt only). Category 3, avoid for now (unchanged).

**Latest results**
- September quarter: revenue Rs 20.94bn (+28%), gross margin 28.0% (32.3%), profit attributable Rs 0.866bn (Rs 1.000bn), EPS Rs 1.96 (Rs 2.27).
- Six months: revenue Rs 36.78bn (+27%), profit from operations Rs 2.69bn (Rs 2.77bn), finance costs Rs 0.87bn (+25%), EPS Rs 3.41 (Rs 3.79).
- Inventories Rs 10.94bn at September (Rs 8.87bn in March, Rs 5.65bn a year before that). Operating cash after interest and tax Rs 1.27bn in the half.
- Capex paid Rs 0.49bn in the half (Rs 3.82bn a year earlier). Borrowings and overdrafts Rs 16.87bn; net debt including leases Rs 15.57bn, 0.49× equity.

**Valuation (Rs a share: bear / base / bull → weighted)**
| Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whole-company DCF | −2.94 | 1.67 | 39.88 | 7.93 |
| P/E | 14.44 | 21.82 | 29.89 | 21.22 |
| Justified P/B | 16.11 | 28.07 | 44.62 | 27.79 |
| Residual income | 14.35 | 21.11 | 31.63 | 21.19 |
| Dividend model | 11.93 | 18.99 | 27.67 | 18.61 |
| Average | 10.78 | 18.33 | 34.74 | **19.35** |

Weights bear 30 / base 50 / bull 20. NAV Rs 72.51 is shown for reference, not averaged.

**Assumptions**
- Required return: risk-free 8.24% (12.24% bond less 4.0% default spread) + beta 1.19 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 20.5%; bear 22.0%, bull 19.0%. WACC 17.1% / 16.0% / 15.0% (debt 31% of value, cost of debt 8.97% before tax).
- DCF: after-tax operating profit Rs 3.27bn (twelve months to September, taxed at 30.1%; bear 10% lower), plus depreciation, less maintenance capex Rs 2.29bn (bull Rs 1.44bn); growth 2% / 6% / 9% for five years, then 4% / 5% / 6%; return on new capital 8% / 10% / 13%. Net debt Rs 15.57bn is taken off.
- EPS to March 2027: Rs 5.20 / 6.20 / 6.80. The run-rate is Rs 7.84 (September quarter × 4), but July–September is the seasonal peak: last year it gave Rs 2.27 of Rs 5.83, and the cyclone-hit second half only Rs 2.04.
- Long-run ROE 8% / 11% / 14% (2023/24–2025/26: 8.8%, 11.5%, 8.1%; six-year average about 12%). Long-term growth 4% / 5% / 6%, below the bond yield and WACC.
- Dividend: Rs 2.00 / 2.50 / 2.75 next year, growing 2% / 5% / 8%.
- Growth check: supported growth 15.1% (2025/26 reinvestment 186% of after-tax operating profit × 8.1% return on capital). That figure is swollen by the vessel and Rs 3.66bn of extra working capital, but every scenario is below it.
- Capex: 2025/26 capex booked Rs 4.81bn was mostly growth (Rs 3.37bn of vessel and dry docking), judged on its return: so far the vessel hasn't lifted margins. Depreciation (Rs 2.29bn) is used as maintenance. Approved but uncommitted capex Rs 1.22bn.

**What would change the view**
Higher: cement price rises that lift the gross margin above 32% and ROE towards 15%; stock run down and debt repaid; the plant filling up; a lower bond yield or beta.
Lower: price competition from importers and the other local makers; a weaker rupee or higher freight; refinancing Rs 12.6bn of short-term loans at higher rates; dividends kept up with borrowing.

**Buy plan (500 shares)**
200 at up to Rs 19.35, 150 at up to Rs 16.45, 150 at up to Rs 14.51: average Rs 17.03, about Rs 8,514. Not realistic now: the lowest prices of the past 18 months were Rs 68.00 (voting) and Rs 58.00 (non-voting). If the view changes, the non-voting share gives the same profit and dividends for about 18% less.

**Warnings**
Dividends are more than cash after maintenance capex, so the dividend is at risk; the expansion was largely paid for with borrowing (net debt up Rs 4.4bn in 2025/26).

**Who owns it**
The Gnanam family companies hold 50.8% of the voting shares and Mitsubishi UBE Cement's Singapore arm 10.0%. The Employees Provident Fund raised its voting stake to 10.0% by June 2026 (7.8% in March) and also holds 10.0% of the non-voting shares.

Figures from the CSE copies of the reports. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
